pos: n. and a. (ten times ten; in Scripture chiefly a round number of fulness, and the standard unit of military and civil division)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hund, a hundred, with the suffix -red, a reckoning — literally a hundred-count. The Hebrew meah and the Greek hekaton both work the same way in Scripture: less an arithmetical statement than a figure for a complete, satisfying, countable whole.
biblical_def: Hundred is the Bible's first large round number, and it does three kinds of work. It measures the long stretch of God's patience: the LORD tells Abram that his seed “shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs… four hundred years” (Gen 15:13) — a promise whose fulfilment outlasts the man who received it, which is precisely the point. It measures the fulness of a flock or a harvest: the shepherd of Luke 15 has “an hundred sheep” (Luk 15:4), and the round completeness of that hundred is what makes the missing one intolerable; a hundred is a number that notices a subtraction. And it measures the sealed people of God, where the hundred is multiplied into the hundred and forty and four thousand of Rev 7:4 — twelve squared and multiplied by a thousand, a number built out of hundreds to say that not one tribe and not one soul has been miscounted. The pattern holds even where the hundred rebukes: Abraham is “an hundred years old” (Gen 17:17) when the promise of Isaac lands, and the number that ought to have closed the womb is the number God chooses to open it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hundred as the product of ten multiplied by ten, and notes its ancient use as a civil division of a county — a district originally supposed to contain a hundred families.
webster_full: HUNDRED, a. Denoting the product of ten multiplied by ten, or the number of ten times ten; as a hundred men.
HUNDRED, n. A collection, body or sum, consisting of ten times ten individuals or units; the number 100.
2. A division or part of a county in England, supposed to have originally contained a hundred families, or a hundred warriors, or a hundred manors.
Note. In Scripture the word is often used indefinitely for a large or complete number, as in the hundredfold of the parable.
scriptures: And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years;
Luk 15:4
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?
Rev 7:4
And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel.
Then Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?
corruption_summary: Biblical numbers are treated either as sloppy exaggeration or as a cipher to be decoded — both of which excuse the reader from the plain reckoning the text actually makes.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors do the same damage. The first treats every large biblical figure as ancient hyperbole, so that four hundred years in Gen 15:13 becomes a storyteller's flourish rather than a term God set and kept; the second treats the numbers as a lock to be picked, hunting a hidden meaning in the digits while the text's own arithmetic goes unread. Scripture uses hundred plainly. Abram is told a span, and Exodus 12:41 reports its close to the day.

The round hundred also carries a pastoral weight the modern eye misses. A shepherd with a hundred sheep has a number he can hold in his head, and that is why the one is missed. Reduce the hundred to a rhetorical flourish and the parable loses its hinge: the Lord is not describing a vague abundance but an exact flock, out of which He knows the precise absence. The doctrine of particular redemption stands on that kind of counting — the Good Shepherd loses none of what the Father gave Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew meah (H3967), a hundred; Greek hekaton (G1540), a hundred, and hekatontaples-type compounds behind “an hundredfold”; the round hundred also underlies the Hebrew military “captains of hundreds”.
roots_lines: Hebrew meah (H3967) — a hundred; the base of the four hundred years of Gen 15:13 and of the hundreds in the census lists.
Hebrew sar meoth — “rulers of hundreds” (Exo 18:21), the second rank in Jethro's ordering of Israel; the hundred is a unit of governance before it is a unit of arithmetic.
Greek hekaton (G1540) — a hundred; the hundred sheep of Luk 15:4 and the hundred pence of Mat 18:28.
Greek hekatontarches (G1543) — centurion, a ruler of a hundred; the Roman office through which the Gospels repeatedly show Gentile faith.
The hundred multiplied — 144,000 in Rev 7:4 is twelve times twelve times a thousand, a completeness built by multiplication, not an inventory of survivors.
usage: “Four hundred years” — a promise God set as a term and kept to the day.
“Having an hundred sheep” — a round flock is a flock that notices one missing.
“An hundred years old” — the number that closes a womb by nature is the number God opens by grace.

pos: n. and a. (ten hundred; in Scripture the standard figure for an uncountable abundance and for a divine reckoning of time)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon thusend, akin to the Gothic thusundi, thought to mean a swollen hundred — the hundred grown past holding. The Hebrew eleph is the same idea from the other side: it is also the word for a clan or a company, so that a thousand in Israel is not first a figure but a body of men.
biblical_def: The thousand is where Scripture's counting passes out of the reader's hand and into God's. It measures His ownership: “every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psa 50:10) — a rebuke to any worshipper who imagines he supplies God with anything. It measures His relation to time: “a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past” (Psa 90:4), which Peter takes up and turns both ways — “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2Pe 3:8). Moses uses the thousand to shrink man; Peter uses it to explain God's apparent slowness, which is longsuffering and not delay. And in the Hebrew census the eleph is a fighting company, so that Israel's thousands are ranks of real men under real captains. The thousand is therefore never merely large: it is the point at which the creature's arithmetic gives out and the Creator's does not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a thousand as the number of ten hundred, and notes at once its proverbial use to signify a great but indefinite number.
webster_full: THOUSAND, n. The number of ten hundred.
2. Proverbially, a great number, indefinitely.
THOUSAND, a. Consisting of ten hundred in number.
2. Proverbially, denoting a great number. He is one of a thousand.
scriptures: Psa 90:4
For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.
But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills.
Rev 7:4
And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand of all the tribes of the children of Israel.
corruption_summary: Psa 90:4 and 2Pe 3:8 are pressed into service as a formula for converting the Bible's days into geological ages — a use neither text will bear.
corruption_paragraphs: Neither verse offers an exchange rate. Moses is contrasting the everlasting God with grass that withers before evening; Peter is answering scoffers who mistake God's patience for slackness, and he says the thousand and the day are alike to the Lord in both directions — which is a statement about God's relation to duration, not a coefficient for reinterpreting Genesis 1. Taking the phrase as arithmetic requires ignoring the word as, which is a simile and not an equals sign.

The other misuse runs the opposite way, taking the thousand years of Revelation 20 as an exact civil calendar to be plotted against current events. The dictionary holds the millennial question open among amillennial, postmillennial, and historic premillennial readings, and rejects the dispensational chart-making that turns the number into a schedule. What Psa 50:10 settles is more urgent than either dispute: the God who owns the cattle upon a thousand hills is not enriched by our offerings and not impoverished by our withholding.
roots_summary: Hebrew eleph (H505), a thousand — also a clan, family, or military company; Greek chilioi (G5507), a thousand, and chilias (G5505), a company of a thousand.
roots_lines: Hebrew eleph (H505) — a thousand; the same consonants also give alluph, a chief, and the word for a clan — a thousand in Israel is a body of men before it is a figure.
Hebrew sar alaphim — “rulers of thousands” (Exo 18:21), the highest rank in Jethro's ordering; the thousand is the largest unit a single man is given to shepherd.
Greek chilioi (G5507) — a thousand; the thousand years of Rev 20.
Greek chilias (G5505) — a group of a thousand; the twelve thousand of each tribe in Rev 7.
Greek chiliarchos (G5506) — a chief captain over a thousand, the officer who rescues Paul in Act 21:31-33.
usage: “The cattle upon a thousand hills” — God is owner, not debtor, in every act of worship.
“A thousand years… as yesterday” — a simile for God's eternity, not a formula for dating.
“Rulers of thousands” — the thousand as a company of men under one captain.

pos: n. and a. (twice ten; in the Law, the age at which a man is numbered, taxed, and mustered)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon twentig — twain plus -tig, a group of ten; literally two tens. The Hebrew esrim is likewise the plural of eser, ten.
biblical_def: Twenty is the threshold number of the Law. “Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the LORD” (Exo 30:14) — at twenty a man enters the census, pays the atonement money, and becomes liable to the muster of war. Twenty is the age at which Israel stops counting a man as a child and starts counting him as one of the people, with a name in the roll and a half shekel to render. That cuts both ways: the wilderness generation condemned at Kadesh is reckoned “from twenty years old and upward” (Num 14:29), so the same threshold that confers standing confers accountability. Twenty appears again in the pleading of Abraham, where it is the second-to-last step of his descent: “Peradventure there shall be twenty found there” (Gen 18:31) — and the LORD grants it, as He grants every step, because the whole exchange is a lesson in how far mercy will go when it is asked.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines twenty as twice ten, and observes that it is used proverbially for an indefinite number, as when we say a thing has been done twenty times.
webster_full: TWENTY, a. Twice ten; as twenty men; twenty years.
2. Proverbially, an indefinite number. He has done it twenty times.
TWENTY, n. The number of twenty; twice ten.
Note. In the Mosaic law, twenty years is the age at which a male is enrolled and numbered among the people.
scriptures: Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the LORD.
And he said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord: Peradventure there shall be twenty found there. And he said, I will not destroy it for twenty's sake.

This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD.
Num 4:3
From thirty years old and upward even until fifty years old, all that enter into the host, to do the work in the tabernacle of the congregation.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; what is lost is the older instinct that a man arrives at a definite age with definite obligations attached.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody disputes the meaning of twenty. What has quietly disappeared is the thing the number does in the Law: mark a line at which a man is enrolled, taxed, and mustered, and after which the excuses of boyhood are no longer available to him. Exo 30:14 hands the twenty-year-old a bill he must pay in person — the same half shekel from rich and poor — and Num 14:29 hands the same generation a judgment it cannot shift onto its parents.

The principle to recover is that Scripture attaches responsibility to an age and expects men to arrive there. A culture that stretches adolescence into the late twenties has not been kinder to its young men; it has withheld from them the standing Exodus grants at twenty. Fathers and elders serve them best by naming the threshold plainly and putting real weight on the other side of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew esrim (H6242), twenty, the plural of eser, ten; the age of enrolment in the Mosaic census and of liability to the atonement money.
roots_lines: Hebrew esrim (H6242) — twenty; grammatically the plural of eser, ten, as the Hebrew tens are all formed.
Hebrew gerah (H1626) — the smallest weight; twenty gerahs make the sanctuary shekel (Exo 30:13), so twenty is also a standard of the sanctuary's own reckoning.
Greek eikosi (G1501) — twenty; used of the four and twenty elders of Rev 4:4.
The muster formula — “from twenty years old and upward, all that are able to go forth to war” (Num 1:3) recurs through the census chapters as a fixed legal phrase.
The judgment formula — the same threshold defines who dies in the wilderness (Num 14:29); standing and accountability are granted together.
usage: “From twenty years old and above” — the age of enrolment, taxation, and muster.
“A shekel is twenty gerahs” — twenty as a standard of sanctuary weight.
“For twenty's sake” — the second-to-last step of Abraham's pleading, and granted.

pos: n. and a. (three times ten; in Scripture the age of entrance into public office, and the price of a slave)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon thritig — three plus the group-of-ten suffix. Hebrew sheloshim is the plural of shalosh, three, on the same pattern.
biblical_def: Thirty is the age at which Scripture puts a man forward. The Levite enters the tabernacle service “from thirty years old and upward” (Num 4:3); Joseph is “thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh” (Gen 41:46); David begins to reign at thirty (2Sa 5:4); and Luke marks the beginning of the Lord's public ministry with the same figure — “Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age” (Luk 3:23). Ten years past the muster-age of twenty, thirty is not when a man becomes accountable but when he is judged seasoned enough to bear office. The number then turns bitterly: thirty pieces of silver is the price the chief priests weigh out to Judas (Mat 26:15), and it is exactly the compensation the Law fixes for a slave gored by an ox (Exo 21:32). Zechariah had already called it “a goodly price that I was prised at of them” (Zec 11:13). The age of entering God's service and the price of a slave meet in the same number at the betrayal of Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thirty as thrice ten, or twenty and ten — a plain numeral adjective with no figurative extension of its own.
webster_full: THIRTY, a. Thrice ten; twenty and ten; as the sum of thirty.
THIRTY, n. The number consisting of thrice ten.
Note. Under the Levitical law the priests and Levites entered upon their service at thirty years of age.
Note. Thirty pieces of silver was the legal valuation of a servant, Exod. xxi. 32.
scriptures: Num 4:3
From thirty years old and upward even until fifty years old, all that enter into the host, to do the work in the tabernacle of the congregation.
And Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt.
Luk 3:23
And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli,
And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
corruption_summary: The thirty pieces are read as a sordid detail of Judas's greed, when Scripture presents them as a fixed legal valuation and a fulfilled prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: Treating the thirty pieces as merely a squalid sum obscures what the Gospels are doing with it. Exo 21:32 sets thirty shekels as the price of a servant killed by another man's ox — the compensation owed for a slave. When the chief priests weigh out that figure, they are not haggling; they are pricing the Lord of glory at the statutory rate for a dead bondman, and Matthew reports it in the language of a covenant: “they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver”.

Zechariah 11:12-13 had named both the sum and its destination generations earlier, and Matthew 27:9-10 draws the thread tight. Modern historical-critical readings that treat the correspondence as the evangelist retrofitting a proof-text invert the actual claim of the text, which is that the prophets wrote what God intended to do and the priests did it without knowing they were quoting. The number belongs to the doctrine of providence, not to the psychology of Judas.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheloshim (H7970), thirty, plural of shalosh, three; Greek triakonta (G5144), thirty — the sum in Mat 26:15 answering Zec 11:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheloshim (H7970) — thirty; the Levitical age of entering the tabernacle service (Num 4:3).
Hebrew shalosh (H7969) — three, the root from which the Hebrew thirty is built.
Greek triakonta (G5144) — thirty; both the age of Luk 3:23 and the silver of Mat 26:15.
Exo 21:32 — thirty shekels of silver is the fixed legal valuation of a manservant or maidservant killed by an ox.
Zec 11:12-13 — the prophet is weighed “thirty pieces of silver” and told to cast it to the potter, the prophecy Mat 27:9-10 sees fulfilled.
usage: “From thirty years old and upward” — the age of entering the Levitical service.
“About thirty years of age” — the Lord enters His public ministry at the office-bearing age.
“Thirty pieces of silver” — the statutory price of a slave, paid for the Son of God.

pos: n. and a. (five times ten; the number of release in the Law and of the Spirit's outpouring in the Gospel)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon fiftig — five plus the group-of-ten suffix. Hebrew chamishim is the plural of chamesh, five; the Greek pentekonta gives the New Testament Pentecost, the fiftieth day.
biblical_def: Fifty is the number at which things are let go. Seven sabbaths of years are counted and the fiftieth is the jubile, when the trumpet sounds, debts are cancelled, servants go free, and every man returns to his possession (Lev 25:10). Fifty is likewise where the Levite's active service ends — “from thirty years old and upward even until fifty years old” (Num 4:3) — so that the number closes a term as reliably as thirty opens one. It is the second figure in Abraham's intercession, where he begins high: “Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city” (Gen 18:24). And it reappears in the Lord's parable of the two debtors, where five hundred pence and fifty are alike forgiven, and the point is that the smaller debtor loves less because he reckons he owed less (Luk 7:41). Counted forward from the Passover sabbath, the fiftieth day is Pentecost — the release of the Spirit upon the church, the jubile trumpet answered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fifty as five tens, and notes the scriptural jubilee as the fiftieth year, in which lands reverted and servants were released.
webster_full: FIFTY, a. Five tens; as fifty men.
FIFTY, n. The number of five tens; 50.
2. Among the Jews, the fiftieth year was the jubilee, in which lands reverted to their former owners and servants were set at liberty.
Note. Pentecost, so called from the Greek, is the fiftieth day from the passover sabbath.
scriptures: Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?
Num 4:3
From thirty years old and upward even until fifty years old, all that enter into the host, to do the work in the tabernacle of the congregation.
Luk 7:41
There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.

This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD.
corruption_summary: The jubile is annexed as a proof-text for debt-forgiveness campaigns and land redistribution schemes, cut loose from the covenant and the tribal inheritance that gave it meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation-theology readings and their evangelical imitators lift the fiftieth year out of Leviticus and present it as a divine economic programme for modern states. But the jubile is not a redistribution; it is a restoration. Land in Israel was never alienable in the first place — “the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine” (Lev 25:23) — so what the trumpet did was return each family to an inheritance God had assigned by lot within a tribal covenant that no modern nation possesses. A scheme that takes property from one citizen to give it to another is doing the opposite of what the fiftieth year did.

The principle the fiftieth year does teach is that God sets terms to servitude and debt, that no man's ruin is permanent in a covenant community, and that the church's generosity should have the same flavour of release. Luke 7:41 supplies the spiritual reckoning: the five hundred and the fifty are both forgiven outright, and the danger is not owing much but imagining you owed little.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamishim (H2572), fifty, plural of chamesh, five; Greek pentekonta (G4004), fifty, and pentekoste (G4005), Pentecost, the fiftieth day.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamishim (H2572) — fifty; the year of jubile (Lev 25:10) and the close of Levitical service (Num 4:3).
Hebrew yobel (H3104) — the ram's horn, and by extension the jubile it announced; the fiftieth year is named for the trumpet that opened it.
Greek pentekonta (G4004) — fifty; the lesser debt of Luk 7:41 and the companies of fifty in Mar 6:40.
Greek pentekoste (G4005) — Pentecost, literally “fiftieth”, counted from the sabbath of the Passover week (Lev 23:15-16).
“Captains of fifty” (Exo 18:21; 2Ki 1:9) — the third rank in Israel's ordering of men.
usage: “Until fifty years old” — the number that closes a term of service.
“Fifty righteous within the city” — the first step of Abraham's descending plea.
“The other fifty” — the lesser debtor, and the lesser love that follows a small reckoning of sin.

pos: n. and a. (one of two equal parts; in Scripture the measure of the ransom, of a divided kingdom, and of a shortened time)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon healf, side or half — originally the side of a thing, whence the part. The older sense survives in on my half, that is, on my side, which is our behalf.
biblical_def: Half in Scripture is rarely a casual fraction; it is usually a deliberate measure. The atonement money is fixed at exactly “half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary” (Exo 30:13) — the rich may not give more nor the poor less, so that the ransom for a soul is the one payment in Israel where no man can outbid his brother. Half a kingdom is the extravagant royal oath, offered by Ahasuerus to Esther (Est 5:3) and by Herod to the daughter of Herodias; in both cases the half-kingdom is a king's way of saying anything, and in both cases what is actually asked exposes the asker. And half is the mark of a time cut short: “there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour” (Rev 8:1), the pause before the trumpets, and the “time, times, and an half” of Daniel and Revelation, where the broken seven signals a persecution God has measured and will not let run its full course.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines half as one equal part of a thing divided into two equal parts, and notes the older sense of side surviving in behalf.
webster_full: HALF, n. plu. halves. One equal part of a thing which is divided into two parts, either in fact or in contemplation; a moiety.
2. It is sometimes used for a part not precisely equal, but nearly so.
HALF, a. Consisting of a moiety, or one part of two; as a half pint; a half hour.
Note. The primary sense is side; hence in behalf of, that is, on the side of.
scriptures: This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD.
Est 5:3
Then said the king unto her, What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.
Rev 8:1
And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour.
Every one that passeth among them that are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give an offering unto the LORD.
corruption_summary: The half shekel is read as a temple tax like any other, when its equality is the whole doctrinal point: no man's soul is worth more than his neighbour's.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 30 is explicit that “the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel” (Exo 30:15). Every other offering in Israel scaled with means — a bullock or a pair of turtledoves according to what a man could bring — but the ransom of a soul is fixed and identical, because the thing being ransomed is identical. Treating it as ordinary temple revenue misses that the sum is a sermon on the equal value of every image-bearer and the impossibility of any man ransoming himself by his wealth.

Psalm 49:7-8 draws the conclusion the half shekel implies: “none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him: (for the redemption of their soul is precious…)”. The half shekel was never the actual price; it was a token that a price exists, that it is the same for all, and that it would one day be paid by Another. The dividing of a thing in half in Scripture is very often a way of saying that God has set the limit and the limit holds.
roots_summary: Hebrew chatsi (H2677), half, from chatsah, to divide; Greek hemisus (G2255), half, and the compound hemiorion (G2256), half an hour.
roots_lines: Hebrew chatsi (H2677) — half, a division; from chatsah, to cut in two, the verb used of dividing a company or a spoil.
Hebrew beqa (H1235) — the half-shekel weight itself (Exo 38:26), from a root meaning to cleave; the ransom token by name.
Greek hemisus (G2255) — half; Zacchaeus gives “the half of my goods” to the poor (Luk 19:8).
Greek hemiorion (G2256) — half an hour, used once, at the silence of Rev 8:1.
“A time, and times, and an half” (Dan 12:7; Rev 12:14) — the broken seven, a persecution measured and cut short.
usage: “Half a shekel” — the one offering in Israel that rich and poor pay alike.
“To the half of the kingdom” — the royal oath that means anything, and exposes the asker.
“The space of half an hour” — heaven's silence before the trumpets.

pos: n. and a. (five and ten; the depth of the flood above the mountains, and the reach of a short journey)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon fiftyne — five and ten. Hebrew forms it the same way, chamishah asar, five and ten.
biblical_def: Fifteen is a modest number that Scripture uses at three memorable hinges. In the flood it is a measurement of total covering: “Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered” (Gen 7:20) — the fifteen is given not to impress but to certify that nothing high enough to stand on remained. In the Gospels it fixes a distance that matters pastorally: “Now Bethany was nigh unto Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs off” (Joh 11:18), close enough that many Jews had come to comfort Martha and Mary, and close enough that the raising of Lazarus could not be hidden from the city that would soon condemn the One who raised him. And in Galatians it measures the whole of Paul's first conference with Peter: “I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days” (Gal 1:18) — a fortnight, which Paul cites precisely because it is short, proving that his gospel was not received from the Jerusalem apostles but confirmed by them. Fifteen is also the day of the month on which both the feast of unleavened bread and the feast of tabernacles begin, the full moon of Israel's two great pilgrim feasts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fifteen as five and ten, and notes the fifteenth day of the month as the beginning of the Jewish feasts of unleavened bread and of tabernacles.
webster_full: FIFTEEN, a. Five and ten; as fifteen men.
FIFTEEN, n. The number of five and ten; 15.
Note. The feast of unleavened bread began on the fifteenth day of the first month, and the feast of tabernacles on the fifteenth day of the seventh.
Note. A furlong being the eighth part of a mile, fifteen furlongs is somewhat less than two miles.
scriptures: Gen 7:20
Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered.
Now Bethany was nigh unto Jerusalem, about fifteen furlongs off:
Gal 1:18
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days.
Luk 3:23
And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli,
corruption_summary: Gen 7:20 is the verse most often cited to prove the flood narrative absurd, which mistakes a plain measurement for a scientific claim the text is not making.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary holds a historical worldwide flood, and Gen 7:20 is one of the reasons: the verse reports a depth, which is the language of a witness, not of legend. The standard objection treats the fifteen cubits as physically impossible and therefore the narrative as mythological material — a move that decides the historicity question before examining it. Moses gives the figure the way a man gives a river's crest: as the measure by which it was known that every high place was covered.

Joh 11:18 shows the same evangelistic habit of exactness. John pauses the most dramatic sign in his Gospel to tell the reader how far Bethany stood from Jerusalem, because the distance explains the crowd, the crowd explains the report that reached the Sanhedrin, and that report explains the council of Joh 11:47-53. What reads as an incidental detail is a hinge of the narrative. Precision in small numbers is a mark of testimony, and it is the historical-critical reflex, not the text, that treats it as decoration.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamishah asar (H2568 with H6240), five and ten; Greek dekapente (G1178), ten and five — the Greek stacks the tens first, the Hebrew the units.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamishah asar — literally “five ten”; the compound behind the fifteenth day of the month.
Greek dekapente (G1178) — fifteen; used of the furlongs of Joh 11:18 and the days of Gal 1:18.
Hebrew ammah (H520) — the cubit, roughly eighteen inches, the unit of Gen 7:20.
Greek stadion (G4712) — the furlong, about an eighth of a Roman mile; fifteen of them is a walk of under two miles.
The fifteenth day — unleavened bread (Lev 23:6) and tabernacles (Lev 23:34) both open at the full moon, on the fifteenth.
usage: “Fifteen cubits upward” — a crest measured, so that no high place remained.
“About fifteen furlongs off” — near enough that the sign could not be hidden.
“Abode with him fifteen days” — short by design, and Paul's proof of an independent gospel.

pos: a. (the ordinal of fourteen; in the Law, the fixed day of the Passover)
etymology: From fourteen with the ordinal ending -th. In Hebrew the ordinal above ten is simply the cardinal used ordinally, arbaah asar, four and ten.
biblical_def: Fourteenth is one of the most legally fixed words in the Old Testament, because it names the day on which the Passover lamb dies. The lamb is taken on the tenth of the first month and kept up “until the fourteenth day of the same month: and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening” (Exo 12:6). Leviticus repeats it as statute: “In the fourteenth day of the first month at even is the LORD'S passover” (Lev 23:5). The date does not float. It survives the wilderness, the conquest, the divided kingdom, Hezekiah's and Josiah's reformations, and the return from exile; and it is the day on which the Lord Jesus is crucified, so that the antitype falls on the calendar the type had held for fifteen centuries. Paul draws the conclusion without argument: “Christ our passover is sacrificed for us” (1Co 5:7). The fourteenth is God's appointment, kept by God, in the death of God's Son.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives fourteenth as the ordinal of fourteen, the fourth after the tenth, and notes the fourteenth day of the first month as the day of the Jewish passover.
webster_full: FOURTEENTH, a. The ordinal of fourteen; the fourth after the tenth.
2. Making one of fourteen equal parts into which a whole is divided.
Note. The passover was killed on the fourteenth day of the first month, at even. Exod. xii. 6; Lev. xxiii. 5.
Note. The second passover, for such as were unclean, was kept on the fourteenth day of the second month. Num. ix. 11.
scriptures: Exo 12:6
And ye shall keep it up until the fourteenth day of the same month: and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening.
Lev 23:5
In the fourteenth day of the first month at even is the LORD'S passover.
Gen 7:20
Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered.
Gal 1:18
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and abode with him fifteen days.
corruption_summary: The fixed date is dissolved into a general theme of liberation, so that the Passover becomes a symbol of freedom in the abstract rather than an appointed sacrifice on an appointed day.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation-theology treatments of the Exodus habitually retain the deliverance and discard the lamb. But Exo 12 puts the blood before the departure: Israel is not freed and then given a ritual to remember it by; Israel is spared on the fourteenth because a substitute died in the house, and the going out follows. Strip the date and the lamb, and what remains is a political parable that could be told about any oppressed people, which is precisely why the framework finds it useful and precisely why it is not what Moses wrote.

The exactness of the fourteenth also answers a subtler corruption: the notion that typology is a devotional overlay the church invented after the fact. A statute given in Egypt, repeated in Leviticus, and kept for centuries fixed the calendar square on which the crucifixion would fall. Neither Israel nor the Sanhedrin arranged that. It is the plainest available evidence that the Old Testament's furniture was built to a plan, and that the plan was the cross.
roots_summary: Hebrew arbaah asar (H702 with H6240), four and ten, used ordinally for the fourteenth day; Greek tessareskaidekatos (G5065), fourteenth.
roots_lines: Hebrew arbaah asar — “four ten”; Hebrew uses the cardinal for ordinals above ten, so the fourteenth day is simply the day “four and ten”.
Hebrew pesach (H6453) — passover, from pasach, to pass or leap over; the feast named for what the LORD did on that night.
Hebrew ben haarbayim — “between the evenings”, the KJV's “in the evening” of Exo 12:6, the interval in which the lamb is killed.
Greek tessareskaidekatos (G5065) — fourteenth; used by Luke of the day of the shipwreck watch (Act 27:27, 33).
Num 9:11 — the second passover, for the unclean and the traveller, on the fourteenth of the second month; the day is moved but never the date within the month.
usage: “Until the fourteenth day of the same month” — the lamb kept four days, then killed.
“In the fourteenth day… is the LORD'S passover” — a statute, not a custom.
The fourteenth of Abib — the calendar square on which type and antitype meet.

pos: n. (a step; hence rank or station in society, and the standing a man attains before God and men)
etymology: From Old French degre, a step or stair, from Latin de- down and gradus, a step. The literal stair survives in the Songs of Degrees, the Psalms of Ascent sung going up to Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Degree in the Authorized Version is a step, and therefore a station. Its commonest use is social: “men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie” (Psa 62:9) — David weighing both ends of the social stair and finding the whole ladder lighter than vanity when set in God's balance. Mary sings the same reversal in the Magnificat: God “hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree” (Luk 1:52). But Paul gives the word its most striking turn, applied not to birth but to faithful service: “they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus” (1Ti 3:13). The degree a man cannot inherit or buy, he may earn by serving tables well — and what he gains by it is not promotion in the church but boldness before God. Fifteen Psalms bear the title A Song of Degrees, the steps by which the pilgrim went up; the word keeps its stair in every use.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines degree first as a step, as of a stair, and then as station, rank, or quality — the measure of a man's place in society or in a scale.
webster_full: DEGREE, n. A step; a distinct portion of space of indefinite extent; a division of a line or of a series.
2. A step or portion of progression, in elevation, quality, dignity or rank; as a man of great degree.
3. Measure; extent; as in some degree.
4. Rank; station; as men of high degree, and men of low degree.
Note. Songs of degrees, the fifteen psalms sung by the Jews in going up to Jerusalem, or upon the steps of the temple.
scriptures: For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Psa 62:9
Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.
Luk 1:52
He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
Est 5:3
Then said the king unto her, What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom.
corruption_summary: 1Ti 3:13 is read as a career ladder — the deacon's office as a rung toward eldership — which reverses Paul's meaning and imports corporate ambition into the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is regularly quoted to make the diaconate a training grade for the eldership, as though a man serves tables in order to be promoted. Paul says nothing of the kind. The good degree is purchased by using the office well, and what it purchases is named in the same breath: “great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus”. The standing is before God and in the confidence of the congregation, not a step on an organisational chart. A church that treats deacons as apprentice elders has already misread the two offices the New Testament actually gives it.

Psa 62:9 supplies the corrective for the wider ambition. David does not say the low are vanity and the high are substantial; he says both ends of the stair are light, and the man who spends his life climbing has weighed the wrong thing. The Magnificat says God Himself moves men up and down the degrees at His pleasure. Rank exists and Scripture acknowledges it — masters and servants, rulers and subjects, elders and flock — but no degree of it survives the balance, and the only elevation worth purchasing is boldness before God.
roots_summary: Hebrew maalah (H4609), a step, stair, or ascent — the word behind “Song of Degrees”; Greek bathmos (G898), a step or standing, used once, at 1Ti 3:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew maalah (H4609) — a step or stair; the steps of Ahaz's dial (2Ki 20:9-11) and the title of the fifteen Songs of Degrees.
Hebrew alah (H5927) — to go up; the root of maalah, and the verb of pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
Greek bathmos (G898) — a step, hence rank or standing; only at 1Ti 3:13, of what a faithful deacon gains.
KJV “low degree” renders Hebrew bene adam (sons of Adam, common men) against bene ish (sons of rank) in Psa 62:9 — the two ends of the stair.
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — lowly, of low degree; the word Mary's song uses of those God exalts (Luk 1:52).
usage: “A good degree” — standing purchased by faithful service, not by promotion.
“Men of low degree… men of high degree” — both ends of the ladder weighed and found light.
“A Song of Degrees” — the steps of the pilgrim going up to the house of the LORD.

pos: n. and a. (nine times ten; the age at which nature had closed the promise, and the number the shepherd leaves behind)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon nigontig — nine plus the group-of-ten suffix. Hebrew tishim is the plural of tesha, nine.
biblical_def: Ninety occurs at two of the most searching places in Scripture. It is Sarah's age when the promise of Isaac is renewed: Abraham falls on his face and laughs, saying in his heart, “Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?” (Gen 17:17). The number is given so the reader can do the arithmetic and reach the same conclusion Abraham reached — and then watch God overturn it. Romans 4:19 makes the point explicit: Abraham “considered not his own body now dead… neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb”; the ninety is the deadness, and faith is what looks at it and still believes the Promiser. The second occurrence is the ninety and nine of the parable: the shepherd “doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?” (Luk 15:4). Here ninety-nine is the number that nearly makes a hundred and therefore will not do — a flock all but complete is a flock with a hole in it, and the Good Shepherd does not settle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ninety as nine times ten, a plain numeral; it is chiefly known in Scripture from the age of Sarah and from the ninety and nine of the parable.
webster_full: NINETY, a. Nine times ten; as ninety men.
NINETY, n. The number of nine times ten; 90.
Note. Sarah was ninety years old when the birth of Isaac was promised. Gen. xvii. 17.
Note. The ninety and nine, in the parable of the lost sheep, denote the flock left in the wilderness while the shepherd seeks the one that is lost. Luke xv. 4.
scriptures: Then Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?
Luk 15:4
What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?
Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?
Psa 90:4
For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.
corruption_summary: The ninety and nine are sentimentalised into the merely respectable, and the lost sheep into a seeker — which turns a parable about sovereign pursuit into a parable about a wanderer's initiative.
corruption_paragraphs: The common reading makes the ninety-nine the self-righteous Pharisees and the one a sincere seeker, and lands on a moral about not judging. Luke sets the parable in a different frame: the Pharisees murmured that Christ receiveth sinners, and eateth with them (Luk 15:2), and the Lord answers by describing a shepherd who leaves the flock and goes after the lost one until he find it. The sheep does not find its way back. It is sought, found, laid on shoulders, and carried — the plainest picture of effectual grace in the Gospels.

Gen 17:17 corrects the parallel error about faith. Abraham laughs; the number is against him; and Scripture nevertheless holds him up as the pattern of believing. Faith in the Bible is not optimism about the odds — a ninety-year-old womb has no odds. It is confidence in the character of the One who promised, which is why Paul says Abraham was “fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform” (Rom 4:21).
roots_summary: Hebrew tishim (H8673), ninety, plural of tesha, nine; Greek enenekonta (G1768), ninety, appearing in the New Testament only in the phrase “ninety and nine”.
roots_lines: Hebrew tishim (H8673) — ninety; Sarah's age at the renewal of the promise (Gen 17:17).
Greek enenekonta (G1768) — ninety; in the New Testament only with ennea, nine, in the “ninety and nine” of Mat 18:12-13 and Luk 15:4, 7.
Rom 4:19 — “the deadness of Sarah's womb”; the apostle's own commentary on what ninety years meant.
Heb 11:11 — Sara “received strength to conceive seed, and was delivered of a child when she was past age”.
The ninety and nine are “in the wilderness” (Luk 15:4) — left in open pasture, not abandoned; the shepherd's errand costs the flock nothing.
usage: “Sarah, that is ninety years old” — the deadness against which faith believes.
“The ninety and nine” — a flock all but complete, which will not satisfy the Shepherd.
“Until he find it” — the sheep is sought and carried, not merely welcomed back.
